newsitem.title: INDIA: India GDP above predictions, to help industry.
newsitem.headline: India GDP above predictions, to help industry.

text.p: India released on Wednesday revised economic growth figures for the past financial year that went above recent predictions, and analysts said the data augured well for industrial growth in the current year.
The government said the revised estimate for gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 1996/97 (April-March) over the previous year was unchanged from last January's forecast of 6.8 percent.
The figure was above predictions of 6.2-6.3 percent made by finance ministry officials last month and stemmed from higher-than-expected agricultural growth that offset lower industrial growth.
But a leading economist cautioned GDP could still be revised lower in final figures. In 1995/96, GDP grew 7.1 percent.

Manoshi Roy, senior director at the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), told Reuters that higher agricultural growth of 5.7 percent, well above the January forecast of 3.7 percent, would lower food bills and boost industrial demand in 1997/98.
"They (people) will have a lot money in their hands to buy industrial products which is a very good thing," Roy said. "Consumer durables should pick up."
But she added the government, aiming for seven percent GDP growth in 1997/98, must boost investment in infrastructure to improve growth in the manufacturing sector.
Growth of this sector was estimated at 8.1 percent in 1996/97 against an earlier forecast of 10.6 percent and down from 13.6 percent in 1995/96.

"The very fact that infrastructure was performing poorly pulled down manufacturing growth," Roy said, adding low growth was spread around all key infrastructure areas: power, crude, petroleum, ports and railways. The sector entitled "electricity, gas and water supply," representing key infrastructure areas, grew 3.8 percent in 1996/97, down from 9.1 percent in 1995/96.
"The point is that infrastructure should be put in place. Infrastructure is the culprit," Roy said.
The sector "agriculture, forestry and fishing" grew 5.7 percent against a fall of 0.1 percent in 1995/96.
Shashanka Bhide, economist at the National Council for Applied Economic Research (NCAER) said industry would certainly improve in 1997/98, but overall GDP growth could be lower.

"We should expect to see a somewhat better industrial growth. Agriculture would be lower than now reported," he said, adding that high grain output of 198 million tonnes in 1996/97 (July-June) would be difficult to repeat in the current year.
"At this point it does seem like the (GDP) growth rate is likely to be revised downwards...I think 6.8 percent seems somewhat high," Bhide said.
He said weaker investment and export figures could curtail higher growth.
A government statement giving a sectoral breakdown of growth rates indicated that the services sector played a big role in sustaining a forecast of 6.8 percent growth in GDP.

Construction grew 5.5 percent; trade, hotels, transport and communications 8.7 percent; finance, insurance, real estate and business services 6.9 percent; community, social and personal services 5.3 percent.
Higher industrial growth expected in the current year would boost the government's tax revenues and help contain the fiscal deficit, Roy said.
India aims to cut its fiscal deficit to 4.5 percent of GDP in 1997/98, from five percent in 1996/97.
